title: Planckian bounds on thermalization times of strongly coupled open quantum systems
authors: Jesús Jiménez-Rodríguez, John Calsamiglia, Martí Perarnau-Llobet
problem: Is there a minimum time for a quantum system to thermalize at temperature \(T\), of the order of the Planckian time \(\hbar/k_BT\)? For weak coupling to a bath such a bound is known, but when the system is strongly coupled its equilibrium state is the mean-force Gibbs state, the reduced state of the global Gibbs state, and open-system speed limits become trivial as the coupling grows. Does a Planckian bound survive at strong coupling, and when?
result: Requiring the same process to thermalize every Hamiltonian in a small neighbourhood gives, at any coupling, \(\tau\ge\tau_{\rm Pl}\,\chi\), where \(\tau_{\rm Pl}=\hbar\beta\) and \(\chi\) measures how distinguishable the mean-force Gibbs states of nearby Hamiltonians are. In the simplest form \(\tau\ge\tau_{\rm Pl}\,r_\kappa\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\kappa)}\), which needs only one static susceptibility and one equilibrium variance. In fermionic models, the spin–boson model and a spin in a two-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet, strong coupling can lift the Planckian constraint when the equilibrium state keeps little information about the system Hamiltonian, and preserves it when that information sits in observables with large, slow fluctuations.
significance: The bound is computed from equilibrium data alone, without solving the dynamics, and it stays informative at strong coupling where speed limits based on interaction energy vanish. It turns the question of how fast a system can thermalize into a question about the quantum Fisher information of its equilibrium state, and identifies the observables that carry the Planckian constraint, which matters for fast qubit reset and dissipative state preparation.
limitations: The bound constrains how fast information about the Hamiltonian is acquired, not the full relaxation, and need not be tight; it requires robustness of thermalization over a family of Hamiltonians, so it says nothing about preparing one known state. The examples are specific models, and the antiferromagnet case is evaluated by quantum Monte Carlo without access to the real-time dynamics. The authors state that Claude Opus 5.5 was used as a coding assistant for the Monte Carlo and TEMPO computations and to edit the text, with all code reviewed by them.

description: A system with Hamiltonian \(H_S\) couples to a bath through \(V=gV_0\), with no limit on \(g\) or on the bath. The target of thermalization is the mean-force Gibbs (MFG) state \(\tilde\omega(\beta,H_S)=\mathrm{Tr}_B\,\omega(\beta,H_S+H_B+V)\), which differs from the bare Gibbs state at finite coupling. A process thermalizes robustly at time \(\tau\) if, with the bath, interaction and initial state fixed, it brings the system within Bures angle \(\varepsilon\) of the MFG state for every Hamiltonian within \(\delta\) of a reference \(\bar H_S\).

Robustness turns thermalization into an information task: if two Hamiltonians have distinguishable equilibrium states, the process must produce distinguishable final states, and quantum estimation theory limits how fast dynamics can encode the difference. Theorem 1 gives \(\tau\ge\tau_{\rm Pl}\chi\), with \(\chi\) the largest ratio of \(2D(\tilde\omega^{(1)},\tilde\omega^{(2)})-4\varepsilon\) to \(\beta\|H^{(1)}-H^{(2)}\|\). For locally exact thermalization, \(\chi\) becomes \(\max_\kappa\sqrt{\mathcal F_\kappa^{\rm th}}/\beta\), the quantum Fisher information of the MFG family.

The paper evaluates this information without the mean-force Hamiltonian. Differentiating the global Gibbs state gives the static susceptibility \(\xi_{A\kappa}\), an equilibrium correlation averaged over a window of width \(\hbar\beta\), and the Fisher information is \(\max_A\xi_{A\kappa}^2/\mathrm{Var}(A)\). The bound is Planckian when some perturbation fluctuates strongly in equilibrium and stays correlated over the Planckian window.

Open-system speed limits bound the distance travelled divided by an energy fluctuation of \(H_S+V\), which grows with \(g\), so they fade at strong coupling. In a double quantum dot they vanish while the true thermalization time grows; the Planckian bound remains finite there. For the spin–boson model, strong coupling reorganizes where the equilibrium information sits, and in a spin coupled to a 2D antiferromagnet the bound is evaluated from imaginary-time correlations alone.

methods.explanation: A process tuned to one known Hamiltonian could swap in a stored Gibbs state arbitrarily fast. Demanding that one mechanism work for a whole neighbourhood of Hamiltonians excludes this and forces the dynamics to learn the Hamiltonian, so the generalized Heisenberg limit of quantum metrology bounds the time.
math: Let \(H_S=\bar H_S+\delta\kappa\) with \(\|\kappa\|=1\) in the spectral seminorm. Locally exact thermalization requires the dynamical Fisher information of the output family to equal the equilibrium one, \(\mathcal F^{\rm dyn}_\kappa(\tau)=\mathcal F^{\rm th}_\kappa\). The generalized Heisenberg limit gives \(\mathcal F^{\rm dyn}_\kappa(\tau)\le\tau^2\|\kappa\|^2/\hbar^2\), so \[\tau\ \ge\ \hbar\sqrt{\mathcal F^{\rm th}_\kappa}=\tau_{\rm Pl}\,\frac{\sqrt{\mathcal F^{\rm th}_\kappa}}{\beta}.\]

For finite changes, the Bures angle between the two targets must be produced by the dynamics; the angle between evolved states grows at most at the rate set by the Hamiltonian difference, and an error \(\varepsilon\) at each end costs \(2\varepsilon\) in total, giving the \([2D-4\varepsilon]_+\) numerator of \(\chi\). Since \(D\le\tfrac\beta4\|H^{(1)}-H^{(2)}\|\), \(\chi\le\tfrac12-2\varepsilon/(\beta\delta)\), so a nontrivial bound needs \(\varepsilon<\beta\delta/4\). Editorial check: for Gibbs states of a random four-level \(H\) and \(H+0.3\kappa\) at \(\beta=1.3\), the Bures angle is \(0.038\), below \(1.3/4\times0.3=0.0975\).

Editorial remark: the bound is a statement about information acquisition, which is why it does not depend on how strong the coupling is. A fast mechanism must resolve the Hamiltonian; the Planckian time is the cost of resolving energy differences of order \(k_BT\).
methods.transfer: Asking that a process work uniformly over a family of parameters turns many preparation tasks into estimation tasks, where Fisher-information limits apply. The same argument bounds the time of other robust protocols, such as cooling or state stabilization.

methods.technique: Fisher information of the mean-force state from a susceptibility and a variance
methods.explanation: The MFG state is hard to compute, and its dependence on \(H_S\) through a mean-force Hamiltonian is unknown. Differentiating the global Gibbs state instead gives the response of any system observable as an equilibrium correlation, and a variational formula turns responses and variances into bounds on the Fisher information.
math: Since \(\delta\kappa\) enters the total Hamiltonian additively, \(\partial_\delta\mathrm{Tr}[\tilde\omega A]=-\xi_{A\kappa}\) with \[\xi_{A\kappa}=\int_0^\beta d\lambda\,\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[\omega_{\rm tot}\,\Delta A(-i\hbar\lambda)\,\Delta\kappa\bigr],\] the isothermal susceptibility. Equivalently it is the symmetrized autocorrelation averaged against a kernel of width about \(\hbar\beta\), whose Fourier transform is the filter \(\tanh(\beta\hbar\nu/2)/(\beta\hbar\nu/2)\).

Proposition 1: \(\mathcal F^{\rm th}_\kappa=\max_A\xi_{A\kappa}^2/\mathrm{Var}(A)\), and \[\frac{\xi_{\kappa\kappa}^2}{\mathrm{Var}(\kappa)}\le\mathcal F^{\rm th}_\kappa\le\beta\,\xi_{\kappa\kappa}\le\beta^2\mathrm{Var}(\kappa)\le\frac{\beta^2\|\kappa\|^2}4.\] Choosing \(A=\kappa\) gives \(\tau\ge\tau_{\rm Pl}\,r_\kappa\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\kappa)}\), where \(r_\kappa\in(0,1]\) is the normalized autocorrelation of \(\kappa\) averaged over imaginary time. Editorial check: for a random four-level Gibbs state at \(\beta=1.3\), the chain reads \(0.0656\le0.0703\le0.107\le0.174\le0.4225\).

The interpretation follows: the bound is close to Planckian when \(\kappa\) has large equilibrium fluctuations (\(\mathrm{Var}(\kappa)\) near \(1/4\)) that remain correlated over imaginary times up to \(\beta\) (\(r_\kappa\) near 1). Fast decorrelation, as in strongly coupled modes whose fluctuations sit at frequencies above \(k_BT/\hbar\), lowers \(r_\kappa\) and lifts the constraint.
methods.transfer: Expressing a Fisher information through linear-response susceptibilities makes metrological bounds computable with equilibrium methods such as quantum Monte Carlo. The same chain of inequalities bounds parameter sensitivity of any reduced thermal state.
